blocks.text: The Vision API lets a chat completion request include image content alongside text, sent either as a URL or as base64 encoded data directly in the request, letting the model analyze and reason about visual content as part of its response.

This topic covers sending an image by URL versus base64 encoding, mixing text and image content in one message, detail levels and their token cost implications, common use cases, and genuine limitations of vision understanding.
1. What the Vision API Means

blocks.alt: Building on structured outputs, the Vision API adds multimodal input

blocks.text: The Vision API extends the standard chat completion request, covered earlier in this module, to accept image content alongside text, letting the model actually see and reason about visual content as part of generating its response.
2. Sending an Image by URL

blocks.alt: An image URL provided lets the model fetch and analyze it directly

blocks.text: The simplest approach provides a publicly accessible URL pointing to the image, the model fetches and analyzes that image directly, this works well when the image already lives somewhere with a stable, accessible URL.
3. Sending an Image via Base64 Encoding

blocks.alt: An image file held locally gets base64 encoded and sent inline in the request

blocks.text: This connects directly to JSON payloads, covered in an earlier module, when an image exists only locally, not at any accessible URL, encoding it as base64 text and embedding it directly in the request body lets you send it without needing to host it anywhere first.

blocks.text: 4. Mixing Text and Image in One Message

blocks.alt: A text content part and an image content part combine in one message content array

blocks.text: This connects directly to the messages array structure covered in an earlier module, a single message content field becomes an array of parts, some text, some image, rather than a plain string, letting a request naturally combine a written question alongside the actual image being asked about.
5. Detail Levels and Token Cost

blocks.alt: Low detail uses fewer tokens, high detail uses more tokens for finer analysis

blocks.text: This connects directly to token optimization, covered in an earlier module, images consume tokens just like text does, a detail setting lets you choose between a lower cost, coarser analysis and a higher cost, more detailed one, matching the setting to what a specific task actually requires avoids paying for detail that is not needed.

blocks.title: Image token cost is a real, often underestimated expense
blocks.content: Teams new to vision capability sometimes underestimate how much a high volume of detailed image analysis actually costs, checking the specific token cost implications of your chosen detail level before scaling up usage avoids an unpleasant billing surprise.

blocks.text: 6. Common Vision Use Cases

blocks.alt: Reading documents or charts, describing scenes, and reviewing a user interface are common use cases

blocks.text: Common genuinely useful applications include reading and extracting information from documents, charts, or screenshots, describing the general content of a scene, and reviewing a user interface design or screenshot for feedback, all leveraging the model ability to interpret visual content directly.
7. Genuine Limitations

blocks.alt: Precise spatial measurement remains generally unreliable

blocks.text: Vision understanding, while genuinely useful, has real limitations, precise spatial measurement, exact pixel counting, or fine-grained numerical reading from a chart, remains generally unreliable, treating vision output with the same healthy skepticism covered in the earlier Hallucination Reduction topic matters here as much as with text.
8. A Worked Vision API Example

A document processing feature sends a scanned invoice image alongside a text question asking for the total amount and date, receiving back an extracted answer, cross-checking this extracted answer against a second independent method for anything genuinely consequential remains good practice given the limitations covered above.
9. Vision vs Image Generation

The Vision API covers the model analyzing and understanding an existing image, image generation, covered in the next topic, covers the reverse direction, the model actually creating a new image from a text description, these are genuinely distinct capabilities solving different problems.
Worked Example

A team building a receipt processing feature initially trusts vision API extracted totals directly for automated expense reporting without any additional check, an occasional misread digit on a blurry receipt causes a subtly wrong total to flow through the system undetected.

Adding a simple sanity check, flagging any extracted total that seems unusually high or low compared to typical values for manual review, catches this class of error before it causes a real accounting problem, demonstrating why vision output deserves the same validation discipline as any other model generated content.
Common Mistakes

items: Trusting vision API output for precise numerical or spatial tasks without any additional verification
Using a high detail level for every image regardless of whether the task actually requires that level of analysis
Not accounting for the real token cost images add, especially at high volume
Sending a local image without base64 encoding it correctly, or trying to send an inaccessible URL

blocks.text: Practice

Construct a vision request combining a text question with an image sent by URL, then repeat the same request with the image base64 encoded instead, comparing the resulting request structure and confirming both approaches work correctly.
Key Takeaway

The Vision API lets a chat completion combine text and image content in one request, sent either as an accessible URL or base64 encoded data, with a detail level controlling the tradeoff between token cost and analysis quality, genuinely useful for many tasks while still carrying real limitations around precise numerical or spatial accuracy that warrant the same validation discipline as any other model output.
